question: When the intended use of an AI system is listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act, the AI system is automatically high-risk, isn't it? If not, can you explain when that is not the case?
pred_answer: No, an Annex III use does not automatically make an AI system high-risk. Article 6(2) sets the general rule that AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk, but Article 6(3) creates an exception to that rule. The Article 6(3) exception. An Annex III system is not high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons. This includes not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making. The exception applies only if at least one of these four conditions is met. (a) the system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) it is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it is intended to detect decision-making patterns, or deviations from prior patterns, and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or. (d) it is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. The profiling override. Under the last subparagraph of Article 6(3), an Annex III system is always high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons. In that case none of the four conditions can take it out of the high-risk category. Documenting and registering the exception. Under Article 6(4), a provider who relies on the exception must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. The provider must also give that documentation to national competent authorities on request. The exception does not remove the duty to register: the provider must still register itself and the system in the EU database under Article 49(2). The system must actually fit a listed use case. The Article 6(2) route covers only systems that fall within a lettered use case under one of Annex III's eight numbered areas, read against the system's intended purpose. A system that only touches a general area, such as employment or education, is not covered. Some use cases carry their own limits in the wording of Annex III. The biometrics entries (point 1) apply only in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. Biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a person is who they claim to be is excluded from point 1(a). AI systems used to detect financial fraud are excluded from point 5(b). The Annex I route is separate. A system can also be high-risk under Article 6(1), regardless of Annex III, if it is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by Annex I legislation that requires a third-party conformity assessment. The Article 6(3) exception does not apply to that route.

question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
pred_answer: No, the AI system is not "medium risk." The EU AI Act has no medium-risk category, and the operator's AI system is a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1). The AI Act does not take over the medical device's risk class under the MDR. It has its own test, and Article 6(1) sets two conditions that must both be met, whether or not the AI system is placed on the market separately from the device. Safety component of an Annex I product (Article 6(1)(a)). The AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the EU harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or be such a product itself. The Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745 is listed in Annex I, Section A, point 11, so the operator's AI safety component meets this condition. Third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)(b)). That product must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation before being placed on the market or put into service. The operator's device goes through a notified body under the MDR, so this condition is also met. What decides the outcome is whether a third-party assessment is required, not the MDR class label. A device in a "medium" MDR class (for example Class IIa or IIb) is caught because it needs a notified body. A self-certified device that needs no third-party assessment would not meet Article 6(1)(b). The Article 6(3) exemption does not apply. It covers only systems listed in Annex III ("no significant risk of harm" plus one of four conditions). The operator's system is high-risk through the Annex I product route, so the provider cannot use that self-assessment to argue it is not high-risk. What being high-risk means in practice. Requirements. The system must meet the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 (Article 8), including. A risk management system across its lifecycle (Article 9); data governance (Article 10); transparency and instructions for use for deployers (Article 13). One combined assessment. Under Article 43(3), you do not run a separate AI Act procedure. You follow the MDR conformity assessment, and the Section 2 requirements become part of it. Notified body powers. Points 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply. These cover the notified body's access to training, validation and test data sets, its power to require more evidence or run tests itself, and, as a last resort, access to the trained models and their parameters. Which notified body. The operator's MDR notified body may assess the AI requirements only if its compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed when it was notified under the MDR. Opting out of a third-party assessment. Article 43(3) allows this only where the sectoral law permits it based on harmonised standards. The manufacturer must then also apply harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements. Shared documentation. Under Article 8(2), you may fold the AI Act testing, reporting and documentation into the operator's existing MDR files, such as ISO 14971 risk management and ISO 13485 quality management records. Changes after certification. A substantial modification triggers a new conformity assessment (Article 43(4)). Changes you pre-determined at the initial assessment and recorded in the technical documentation under Annex IV, point 2(f) do not count as substantial. Under the Regulation as adopted, the obligations for Article 6(1) high-risk systems apply from 2 August 2027.

question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
pred_answer: The system is not prohibited, and it is not high-risk under Annex III. That holds only while its sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Article 5(1) lists the banned practices, and one-to-one biometric verification is not among them. Article 5(1)(h) bans only the use of "real-time" remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. The exceptions in points (h)(i) to (iii) cover. Targeted searches for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation, and for missing persons; preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or safety, or a terrorist attack; locating or identifying suspects of Annex II offences punishable by at least four years. Verification is not remote identification, so this ban does not reach the operator's system. Article 5(1)(g) bans biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. A system that only confirms a claimed identity does not do this. Article 5(1)(f) bans emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions. Article 5(1)(e) bans untargeted scraping of facial images to build or expand facial recognition databases. Neither applies, provided the system does not infer emotions and its reference templates are not collected that way. Article 6(2) with Annex III point 1(a): point 1(a) lists remote biometric identification systems as high-risk. It expressly states that this "shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be.". Annex III points 1(b) and 1(c): the system is not caught by these either. They cover biometric categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes, and emotion recognition. Because the system is not listed in Annex III, you do not need to rely on this derogation. When the conclusion would change. Extra functions: the exclusion depends on the "sole purpose" condition. If the system also runs one-to-many identification, remote identification, categorisation or emotion recognition, it falls back under Annex III point 1. Product route: separately, under Article 6(1), the system is high-risk if both conditions are met. It is a safety component of a product covered by the legislation listed in Annex I, or is itself such a product; that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Other Annex III uses: if the verification is used for a purpose listed elsewhere in Annex III, that entry must be assessed on its own terms. Transparency and data protection. This duty to inform people applies only to deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems, so it does not apply to the operator. This duty falls on the provider, and only if the system is intended to interact directly with natural persons. Even then, it does not apply where the AI interaction is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person. GDPR: processing the biometric data remains subject to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679.

question: Are AI safety components within medical devices of MDR class IIa, IIb, or III considered to be high-risk according to the EU AI Act? Why?
pred_answer: Yes. An AI system meant to be used as a safety component of a medical device in MDR class IIa, IIb or III is high-risk under Article 6(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. It meets both conditions of that paragraph. The product is covered by Annex I legislation (Article 6(1)(a)). The AI system is intended as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices (MDR) is listed at Annex I, point 11. The same limb applies where the AI system is itself the product, such as software that is a medical device in its own right. The product needs third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)(b)). The product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that Annex I legislation before it is placed on the market or put into service. Under the MDR, devices in classes IIa, IIb and III must have a notified body involved in their conformity assessment. That meets the condition. Class I devices are generally self-certified, so they would not normally meet this condition. No derogation applies. Article 6(1) applies whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service on its own or as part of the device. The exemption for systems that do not pose a significant risk of harm is in Article 6(3). It covers only AI systems listed in Annex III under Article 6(2), so it cannot remove high-risk status from a system classified under Article 6(1). The classification does depend on the AI system actually being a safety component of the device, or the device itself. Annex I status alone does not make every AI function in a device high-risk. Conformity assessment follows the MDR procedure (Article 43(3)). The provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required by the MDR. The requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 of the AI Act apply and form part of that assessment. Annex VII points 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5, and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6, also apply. Notified bodies designated under the MDR may check the AI system against the Section 2 requirements. This is allowed only if their notification procedure assessed them against Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11). If a substantial modification is made, a new conformity assessment is required under Article 43(4). For systems that keep learning after being placed on the market or put into service, changes the provider set in advance are not a substantial modification. They must have been fixed at the initial assessment and recorded in the technical documentation under Annex IV, point 2(f).

question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
pred_answer: Human oversight is governed by Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Under Article 14(1), high-risk AI systems must be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use. Article 14(2) says the aim of oversight is to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. This covers use in line with the intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse, especially where those risks remain despite the other requirements of that Section. Article 14(3) requires oversight measures to be commensurate with the system's risks, level of autonomy and context of use. The measures can take either or both of two forms. Measures the provider identifies and, where technically feasible, builds into the system before it is placed on the market or put into service (point (a)); measures the provider identifies before that point that are appropriate for the deployer to implement (point (b)). Under Article 14(4), the system must be provided to the deployer so that the people assigned to oversight can do the following, as appropriate and proportionate. (a) properly understand the system's relevant capacities and limitations, and duly monitor its operation, including detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance; (b) remain aware of the tendency to rely or over-rely on its output ("automation bias"), in particular where the system provides information or recommendations for decisions taken by natural persons; (c) correctly interpret the output, taking into account the interpretation tools and methods available; (d) decide in any particular situation not to use the system, or to disregard, override or reverse its output; (e) intervene in the system's operation or interrupt it through a "stop" button or similar procedure that brings it to a halt in a safe state. Article 14(5) adds a rule for the remote biometric identification systems in point 1(a) of Annex III. The deployer may not take any action or decision based on an identification from such a system unless at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority have separately verified and confirmed it. This two-person check does not apply to systems used for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum where Union or national law considers it disproportionate.

question: Which AI systems used in education or vocational training should be classified as high-risk according to the EU AI Act?
pred_answer: Under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 3 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, four types of AI system used in education and vocational training are high-risk. Access and admission (Annex III, point 3(a)): systems intended to determine access or admission to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels, or to assign natural persons to them. Evaluating learning outcomes (point 3(b)): systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes, including when those outcomes are used to steer the learning process of natural persons in such institutions. Level of education (point 3(c)): systems intended to assess the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or will be able to access, in the context of or within such institutions. Proctoring (point 3(d)): systems intended to monitor and detect prohibited behaviour of students during tests in the context of or within such institutions. Only these listed uses make an education system high-risk through this route. Other AI used in education is not caught by Annex III, point 3. It can still be high-risk under Article 6(1), but only if both conditions there are met. It is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I, or is itself such a product (for example, a toy under Directive 2009/48/EC, Annex I, point 2); and. That product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. A system that falls under Annex III, point 3 can escape high-risk status under Article 6(3). This applies only if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making. It must also meet one of these conditions. (a) it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) it is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it is intended to detect decision-making patterns, or deviations from prior patterns, and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or. (d) it is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to the Annex III use cases. This exception never applies if the system profiles natural persons. Such a system is always high-risk under the final subparagraph of Article 6(3). Under Article 6(4), a provider that considers an Annex III system not to be high-risk must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. The provider must also register under Article 49(2) and give the documentation to national competent authorities on request.

question: What obligations, if any, does the EU AI Act set in place for AI systems that interact directly with natural persons? What exceptions, if any, apply?
pred_answer: Yes. Under Article 50(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, providers of AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must design and develop them so that the people concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system. The duty is built into the system at design stage and sits with the provider, not the deployer. It applies whether or not the system is high-risk. Article 50(5) sets how the information must be given. It must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner. It must be given at the latest at the time of the first interaction. It must meet the applicable accessibility requirements. Article 50(6) adds that this duty does not affect the requirements and obligations in Chapter III. It is also without prejudice to other transparency obligations for deployers under Union or national law. So a chatbot that is also a high-risk system must meet both sets of rules. Article 50(1) contains two exceptions. Obvious from context: No disclosure is needed where it is obvious that the person is dealing with an AI system. This is judged from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. Criminal law enforcement: The duty does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties. This exception does not apply where such a system is available for the public to report a criminal offence, so a public-facing crime-reporting chatbot must still disclose its AI nature.

question: How does Annex II relate to prohibited uses of AI systems?
pred_answer: Annex II does not list any prohibited practices. It has one narrow job inside Article 5: it is the exhaustive list of criminal offences that can justify an exception to one prohibition. That prohibition, in Article 5(1)(h), bans the use of "real-time" remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Article 5(1)(h) allows such use only where it is strictly necessary for one of three objectives. (i) a targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, or for missing persons; (ii) preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine and present or foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; (iii) locating or identifying a person suspected of a criminal offence, for a criminal investigation, a prosecution or the execution of a criminal penalty. Annex II matters only for objective (iii). The offence must be listed in Annex II and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order with a maximum of at least four years. The Annex II offences are. Terrorism; trafficking in human beings; sexual exploitation of children, and child pornography; illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances; illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives; murder, grievous bodily injury; illicit trade in human organs or tissue; illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials; kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking; crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court; unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships; rape; environmental crime; organised or armed robbery; sabotage; participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of these offences. Annex II has no bearing on the other prohibitions in Article 5(1)(a) to (g). Point (h) is also without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) for processing biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement. Article 5(8) keeps in place any prohibitions that arise where an AI practice breaks other Union law. An Annex II offence is necessary but not enough on its own. Every use must also meet these conditions. Purpose (Article 5(2)): the system may be used only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual. The authority must weigh how serious, likely and large the harm would be without the system, and the consequences for the rights and freedoms of everyone affected. It must also respect the necessary and proportionate safeguards in the national law authorising the use, including limits on time, place and persons. Impact assessment and registration (Article 5(2)): use can be authorised only once the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registered the system in the EU database under Article 49. In duly justified urgent cases, use may start before registration, provided registration is completed without undue delay. Prior authorisation (Article 5(3)): each use needs prior authorisation from a judicial authority, or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, based on a reasoned request. The authority may grant it only if objective evidence or clear indications show the use is necessary and proportionate, and strictly limited in time, place and persons. In a duly justified urgent situation, use may start without authorisation, but authorisation must be requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours. If authorisation is refused, use must stop immediately, and all data, results and outputs must be discarded and deleted. No decision with an adverse legal effect on a person may be based solely on the system's output. Notification (Article 5(4)): each use must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority, without sensitive operational data. National law (Article 5(5)): the exception exists only if a Member State chooses to allow it, fully or partially, in national law. That law must set the detailed authorisation rules and specify which objectives, and which Annex II offences, are covered. It must be notified to the Commission within 30 days of adoption. Member States may also adopt more restrictive rules.

question: Can the European Commission amend Annex III of the EU AI Act to add or modify use-cases classified as high-risk AI systems? Under what conditions?
pred_answer: Yes. Under Article 7(1), the Commission can amend Annex III by adopting delegated acts that add or modify use-cases of high-risk AI systems. It must meet two conditions and follow the procedure in Article 97. Conditions for adding or modifying a use-case (Article 7(1)). Both conditions must be met; neither is enough alone. (a) Existing area: the AI systems are intended to be used in one of the areas already listed in Annex III. (b) Equivalent or greater risk: the AI systems pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to, or greater than, the risk posed by the high-risk AI systems already listed in Annex III. Because of condition (a), the Commission can only add or change lettered use-cases under the eight existing areas. It cannot create a new area by delegated act. Criteria for judging the risk in condition (b) (Article 7(2)). The Commission must take into account. (a) the intended purpose of the AI system. (b) how far the system has been used, or is likely to be used. (c) the nature and amount of data processed, in particular whether special categories of personal data are involved. (d) how autonomously the system acts, and whether a human can override a decision or recommendation that may lead to harm. (e) how far its use has already caused harm or adverse impact, or raised significant concerns, for example through reports or documented allegations to national competent authorities. (f) the potential extent of the harm, in particular its intensity, its ability to affect many people, or its disproportionate effect on a particular group. (g) how dependent affected persons are on the outcome, in particular where they cannot reasonably opt out for practical or legal reasons. (h) any imbalance of power, or how vulnerable affected persons are in relation to the deployer, for example due to status, authority, knowledge, economic or social circumstances, or age. (i) how easily the outcome can be corrected or reversed. Outcomes with an adverse impact on health, safety or fundamental rights are not considered easily correctable or reversible. (j) the size and likelihood of the benefits for individuals, groups or society, including possible improvements in product safety. (k) how far existing Union law provides. (i) effective redress for the risks, excluding claims for damages; (ii) effective measures to prevent or substantially minimise those risks. Removing a use-case (Article 7(3)). The Commission can also remove high-risk AI systems from Annex III, again only if both conditions are met. (a) the system no longer poses any significant risks to fundamental rights, health or safety, judged against the Article 7(2) criteria; and. (b) the removal does not reduce the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights under Union law. Procedure (Article 97). Duration: the power runs for five years from 1 August 2024 (Article 97(2)). The Commission must report on it at least nine months before that period ends. It renews automatically for further five-year periods unless the European Parliament or the Council objects at least three months before a period ends. Revocation: the Parliament or the Council can revoke the power at any time (Article 97(3)). Consultation: before adopting a delegated act, the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State, following the Interinstitutional Agreement of 13 April 2016 on Better Law-Making (Article 97(4)). Notification: once adopted, the act must be notified to the Parliament and the Council at the same time (Article 97(5)). Entry into force (Article 97(6)): the act takes effect only if neither the Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification. That period can be extended by another three months at the initiative of either institution. The act can take effect sooner if both inform the Commission before the deadline that they will not object.

question: Should market surveilance authorities be provided with remote access to documentations and data sets used to develop a high-risk AI system?
pred_answer: Yes. Under Article 74(12), providers of high-risk AI systems must give market surveillance authorities full access to two things. The documentation; the training, validation and testing data sets used to develop the system. That access includes remote access where appropriate. It can be given through application programming interfaces (APIs) or "other relevant technical means and tools enabling remote access". Article 74(12) sets three limits. Relevance and necessity: access applies "where relevant and limited to what is necessary to fulfil their tasks". Appropriateness: remote access is required "where appropriate", not in every case. Security: remote access is "subject to security safeguards". The duty also applies "without prejudice to" the authorities' powers under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. Separately, Article 74(5) lets authorities use the powers in Article 14(4), points (d) and (j), of that Regulation remotely, as appropriate. Access to source code is a separate and narrower right under Article 74(13). The authority must make a reasoned request, and both of these conditions must be met. Access to the source code is necessary to assess whether the system meets the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 (Article 74(13)(a)); testing, auditing and checks based on the data and documentation from the provider have been exhausted or proved insufficient (Article 74(13)(b)). Under Article 74(14), authorities must treat any information or documentation they obtain in line with the confidentiality obligations in Article 78.

question: If a provider of a high-risk AI system confirms that the system achieves an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity at the time of development, then no further action is required by the provider on these aspects in the future. Correct?
pred_answer: No, that is not correct. Confirming adequate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity during development does not end the provider's obligations. Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, these are lifecycle obligations that continue after the system is placed on the market or put into service. Article 15 is a lifecycle duty. Article 15(1) requires high-risk AI systems to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. It also requires them to "perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle." Meeting the level at development is only part of the duty. The other paragraphs point the same way. The provider must declare the levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics in the instructions for use, so deployers can rely on that performance. The system must be as resilient as possible to errors, faults or inconsistencies, including those arising from its interaction with people or other systems. Technical redundancy, such as backup or fail-safe plans, may be used. Systems that keep learning after being placed on the market must be developed to eliminate or reduce the risk that biased outputs feed back into future operations, and such feedback loops must be addressed. The system must be resilient against unauthorised third parties trying to alter its use, outputs or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities. Measures must address data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples or model evasion, confidentiality attacks and model flaws. These threats change over time, so the protection cannot be fixed once. Article 9 requires ongoing risk management. Under Article 9(1), the risk management system must be "established, implemented, documented and maintained." Under Article 9(2), it is a continuous, iterative process that runs throughout the lifecycle and needs regular, systematic review and updating. It includes. Identifying and analysing known and reasonably foreseeable risks (point (a)); estimating and evaluating risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse (point (b)); evaluating other risks that may arise, based on post-market monitoring data (point (c)); adopting appropriate, targeted risk management measures (point (d)). Under Article 9(5), the residual risks must continue to be judged acceptable. Article 17 builds this into the quality management system. Article 17(1) requires the system to cover. Procedures for managing modifications to the high-risk AI system (point (a)); examination, test and validation procedures carried out "before, during and after" development, and how often they are carried out (point (d)); setting up, running and maintaining post-market monitoring (point (h)); reporting serious incidents (point (i)). Article 16 adds continuing provider duties. Providers must keep the system compliant with Section 2, which includes Article 15 (Article 16(1)(a)). They must also take the necessary corrective actions and provide information where the system does not conform (Article 16(1)(j)). Changes and the instructions for use. Under Article 43(4), a substantial modification requires a new conformity assessment. For systems that keep learning, changes the provider pre-determined at the initial conformity assessment, and documented in the technical documentation, do not count as a substantial modification. The instructions for use must include. The level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity that can be expected, and any known and foreseeable circumstances that may affect it (Article 13(3)(b)(ii)); any pre-determined changes (Article 13(3)(c)); the expected lifetime of the system and the maintenance and care measures needed, including software updates (Article 13(3)(e)). Cybersecurity certification. A certificate or statement of conformity under Regulation (EU) 2019/881 gives only a presumption of conformity with the Article 15 cybersecurity requirements, and only to the extent it covers them (Article 42(2)). It does not replace the ongoing lifecycle obligations described above.

question: Are AI systems that fall under one of the areas of Annex III, but not falling within a use-case within such areas, considered high-risk?
pred_answer: No. An AI system that operates in one of the Annex III areas but does not match a use-case listed under that area is not high-risk under the Annex III route. Article 6(2) gives high-risk status to "AI systems referred to in Annex III". Annex III does not name whole sectors. It names specific systems, described by their intended purpose, grouped under eight numbered areas. The area heading only groups the listed use-cases; the listed use-case is what decides classification. The eight areas are. Biometrics. Critical infrastructure. Education and vocational training. Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment. Access to essential private and public services and benefits. Law enforcement. Migration, asylum and border control management. Administration of justice and democratic processes. Some examples. Critical infrastructure (Annex III, point 2): only systems "intended to be used as safety components" in running critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity are covered. An AI tool used by an energy utility for something other than a safety function is not high-risk under Article 6(2). Biometrics (point 1(a)): biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a person is who they claim to be is expressly excluded. Creditworthiness (point 5(b)): systems used to detect financial fraud are expressly excluded. Elections (point 8(b)): tools whose output people are not directly exposed to, such as tools that organise political campaigns administratively or logistically, are expressly excluded. For the same reason, the Article 6(3) derogation and the Article 6(4) duty to document an assessment are not relevant to such a system. They only apply to a system "referred to in Annex III", meaning one that already falls within a listed use-case. The Article 6(3) conditions are a narrow procedural task, improving the result of completed human work, detecting decision-making patterns, or a preparatory task. The profiling rule is part of the same derogation, so it does not apply either. Such a system can still be high-risk by the separate Annex I route under Article 6(1). That applies if it is a safety component of a product covered by the EU harmonisation laws listed in Annex I, or is itself such a product, and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under those laws.

question: If I have an AI system that is high-risk because listed in the use cases of Annex III, and change it to a different use case that is not in Annex I or III, does it stay high-risk due to its historical provenance?
pred_answer: No. Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, an AI system is not high-risk because of what it used to be. Classification depends on what the system is intended to be used for now. If you genuinely change that purpose to one that neither Annex III nor Annex I covers, it is no longer high-risk. Why history doesn't count. question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
pred_answer: Under Article 1(1), the Regulation's purpose is to improve the functioning of the internal market and to promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI. It must do this while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and while supporting innovation. To achieve that purpose, Article 1(2) lays down. (a) harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service and the use of AI systems in the Union; (b) prohibitions of certain AI practices; (c) specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems; (d) harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems; (e) harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models; (f) rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement; (g) measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups.

question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
pred_answer: Under Article 101(5), the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine under Article 101. The Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine. This means the Court is not limited to checking whether the decision is lawful. It can look at the amount again itself and replace the Commission's fine with its own. That includes raising the fine, not only cutting or annulling it. The decisions under review are those made under Article 101(1). There, the Commission may fine providers of general-purpose AI models up to 3% of their total worldwide annual turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher. The fine applies where the Commission finds that the provider, intentionally or negligently. (a) infringed the relevant provisions of the Regulation; (b) failed to comply with a request for a document or for information under Article 91, or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information; (c) failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93; or. (d) failed to give the Commission access to the model, or to the model with systemic risk, for an evaluation under Article 92. When the Court reviews the amount, the same criteria apply as for the Commission. Setting the amount (Article 101(1)): the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, the principles of proportionality and appropriateness, and commitments made under Article 93(3) or in codes of practice under Article 56. Effect of the fine (Article 101(3)): fines must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. Right to be heard (Article 101(2)): before adopting the decision, the Commission must communicate its preliminary findings to the provider and give it an opportunity to be heard.

question: Consider the situation in which a market surveillance authority (MSA) determines that an AI system, originally classified as non-high-risk by the provider, is in fact high-risk. Withdrawal or recall is not automatic. During that period the provider must make sure all necessary compliance action is taken (Article 80(4)). It must also make sure appropriate corrective action covers every affected system it has made available on the Union market (Article 80(5)). If the use of the system is not restricted to the authority's own country, the authority must tell the Commission and the other Member States, without undue delay, what it found and what it required (Article 80(3)). If the provider does not act in time. If the provider fails to take adequate corrective action within the prescribed period, Article 79(5) to (9) applies (Article 80(6)). Under Article 79(5), the authority must then take all appropriate provisional measures. These can prohibit or restrict making the system available or putting it into service, or withdraw or recall it. The authority must notify the Commission and the other Member States without undue delay. If no objection is raised within three months, the measure is deemed justified (Article 79(8)). If one is raised, the Commission decides under Article 81(1). Where gravity matters. Deadline length: Article 80(2) sets no fixed deadline. The authority decides the period case by case, in proportion to the non-compliance and the risk. Systems presenting a risk: If the system also presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights within Article 79(1), the Article 79(2) procedure applies. The authority can require bringing the system into compliance, withdrawal or recall within a period it prescribes. That period can be no longer than 15 working days, or the period set by the relevant Union harmonisation legislation if shorter. Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 governs these measures. Serious incidents: If a serious incident has been reported, the authority must take appropriate measures within seven days of receiving the notification (Article 73(8)). The provider's own duty: Once the provider has reason to consider that its now high-risk system does not conform, it must immediately take the necessary corrective actions (Article 20(1)). The provider must also inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. If the system presents an Article 79(1) risk, it must immediately investigate the causes and inform the competent authorities (Article 20(2)). Deliberate misclassification: If the authority finds the provider misclassified the system to avoid the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2, the provider faces fines (Article 80(7)). Recall, withdrawal or restriction become mandatory only if it fails to act in time, or earlier where the risk requires it.

question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, what is the definition of (a) a "conformity assessment body" and (b) "conformity assessment"?
